summary: Prospect Harbor Point Light, Gouldsboro, Maine: a granite tower of 1849 or 1850, dark from 1859 to 1870, the wooden tower of 1891, automated in 1934, now on a Navy installation.

lens.where: fourth-order Sautter lens installed 1906 (LighthouseFriends); the Fresnel lens was replaced in 1951 (New England Lighthouses)

structures.note: Granite conical tower attached to the stone dwelling; pulled down in 1891 when the buildings were replaced (NRHP).
Conical, shingled wooden tower, 38 ft tall (LighthouseFriends). The record gives 11.5 m. Built about 25 ft south of the 1850 tower.
One-and-a-half-story frame keeper's house, on the foundation of the old stone dwelling (NRHP; Board report 1891-1892). Known as Gull Cottage.
Small stone gable-roofed oil house (NRHP; New England Lighthouses).
Boathouse and boat slip added 1897 (LighthouseFriends); the Board's report for 1896-1897 records a site cleared for it.

access.note: The light stands on the grounds of a U.S. Navy satellite operations installation. The grounds are closed to the public for security reasons. The view is from Route 186 across the harbor and from the entrance to the Navy installation.

facts.agency: U.S. Navy (keeper's dwelling and grounds); U.S. Coast Guard owns the tower, leased to the American Lighthouse Foundation

events.note: Congress authorizes the light station (NRHP)
LighthouseFriends gives 2 April 1849 as the date the light was established; the NRHP, Archive and New England Lighthouses give 1850
Light established; granite tower attached to the stone dwelling
Granite conical tower and stone dwelling
S. H. Sargent succeeds Pillsbury Stevens in April 1853 (New England Lighthouses)
Tower fitted with a new and improved reflecting apparatus (LighthouseFriends)
Fifth-order Fresnel lens installed in the lantern room (LighthouseFriends); the Archive gives 1870 for the original fifth-order lens
Light discontinued by the Light-House Board
Light reestablished from 15 May 1870; buildings renovated
Conical wooden tower, 38 ft, and frame dwelling; old buildings pulled down
Light moved to a new tower about 25 ft south, 25 July 1891 (Board report 1891-1892)
Boathouse and boat slip added
New boat winch furnished (Board report 1900)
Stone oil house
Fifth-order lens replaced by a fourth-order L. Sautter & Co. lens (LighthouseFriends)
Changed from flashing alternately red and white to fixed red with two white sectors (LighthouseFriends)
Light automated; last keeper Albion T. Faulkingham
Fresnel lens replaced (New England Lighthouses)
Keeper's house offered at auction; high bid rejected; property transferred to the U.S. Navy (New England Lighthouses)
NRHP reference 88000151; the nomination's continuation sheet cites Review Comments dated 1/21/88
Coast Guard crew reshingles and repaints the tower (April 2000)
American Lighthouse Foundation takes responsibility for the light from the Coast Guard (May 2000)
Stair renovation begun by the American Lighthouse Foundation
Lantern removed by crane in August 2004, repainted; lantern room restored
Windows replaced with a grant from the New England Lighthouse Lovers
Overnight stays in Gull Cottage end in October 2021 when the property is put under a different military branch (New England Lighthouses)
Fire in the keeper's dwelling on 27 June 2022 while a family was staying there; the fire did not reach the tower

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record and NRHP give 1850 for establishment; LighthouseFriends gives 2 April 1849. The 1850 date is used because the NRHP, the Archive and New England Lighthouses agree on it.
The light remains an active aid to navigation on Navy grounds (New England Lighthouses), and the complex stays in federal ownership (NRHP).
LighthouseFriends: established 2 April 1849; the NRHP, the Archive and NEL: 1850. The opening now says 1849 or 1850 and the story states the disagreement.

The NRHP says the Light-House Board deactivated the light, claiming the harbor was not used as an anchorage during storms; LighthouseFriends says Congress decided to discontinue it after being told the harbor was not used as a harbor of refuge; NEL gives the same reasons with the village's small coasting trade. Stated in the story.
LighthouseFriends: fifth-order lens installed 1857; the Archive: 1870. Stated in the story.
The Archive and LighthouseFriends name Nathaniel Noyes (1849) first; New England Lighthouses names Pillsbury Stevens. Stated in the story.
The Archive and NEL give 1885; LighthouseFriends's text says 1891 but its keeper list and thirty-three-year total fit 1885. Stated in the story.
The Archive and LighthouseFriends: 1930-1934; NEL's keeper list: c. 1928-1935. Stated in the story.
LighthouseFriends and NEL's keeper list: 1953; NEL's text: the mid-1950s. Stated in the story.

notes_for_editor: (1) First keeper: the Archive and LighthouseFriends name Nathaniel Noyes (1849); New England Lighthouses names Pillsbury Stevens, and says Sargent succeeded him in April 1853. Not resolved. (2) Establishment: LighthouseFriends 2 April 1849; NRHP, Archive, NEL 1850; the NRHP says authorized 1847. (3) Original fifth-order lens: LighthouseFriends 1857; the Archive 1870. Not resolved. (4) Wasgatt's start: LighthouseFriends text says 1891, its keeper list and its 'thirty-three years' say 1885; the Archive and NEL say 1885. (5) Record's focal height 12.8 m vs the Archive's 43 ft (13.1 m) for the current light: not used. (6) Record's characteristic 'Fl W 6s' is not verified against the Light List: not used; LighthouseFriends reports 'fixt red with two white sectors' from 1906. (7) Stays: New England Lighthouses says the Gull Cottage program ended October 2021; LighthouseFriends (older) says the dwelling could be reserved. Stay set to null; verify before any stay is listed. (8) No storm, wreck or rescue at the station is recorded in the sources read, so the storms chapter is omitted. The Life-Saving Service tables list 'Prospect Harbor' among places where vessels stranded, but the OCR columns do not give reliable per-year counts for it. A Chronicling America search for Wasgatt returned local news; a lighthouse-specific search timed out. (9) Access: the Archive says 'Open to Public: No'; LighthouseFriends says 'Grounds/dwelling/tower closed'; NEL says grounds off limits. (10) LighthouseFriends' ghost legends (Travel Channel 2004) are left out as legend, not history. (11) Family members named in the sources (the Wasgatt daughters and granddaughter, the Faulkingham and Workman families, the 2022 family staying in the dwelling) are not named; the Workman family's personal details are left out. (12) Ira Winn, listed as a contractor in the Archive, is left out as Orne was for Perkins Island. (13) The Board's dwelling and move entries were matched by the scan pages in the 1891-1892 volume; printed page numbers were not read. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-22 (Haiku fact-checker): (a) Fiscal-year labels: 'old and dilapidated' is in the fiscal-1891 report (scan 48); the relocation (25 July 1891) and the new dwelling (19 by 20 feet) are in the fiscal-1892 report (scan 341 and 373); the boathouse site is in the fiscal-1897 report (scan 292); the new boat winch is in the fiscal-1900 report (scan 47). (b) The Wasgatt retirement age (72) is taken from New England Lighthouses' passage about a granddaughter's father, which is ambiguous as to whose father is meant; left out. (c) The 1870 relight reason is 'for some as yet unknown reason' (NRHP); the story quotes it rather than giving a cause. (d) The 2022 fire: LighthouseFriends says a family of four staying in the dwelling was awakened by smoke detectors; the family is not named and nothing about them is added. (e) Unresolved: first keeper Noyes (Archive, LighthouseFriends) vs Pillsbury Stevens (NEL). Stated. (f) The Coast Guard's 2000 work and the 2001 and 2004 ALF work follow New England Lighthouses. The Navy's ownership of the dwelling follows the Archive and LighthouseFriends.
